title: Hyper-V in Plain English
summary: Understand Hyper-V as a type-1 virtualization platform and distinguish host, hypervisor and guest responsibilities.
plain_language_explanation: Hyper-V lets one physical Windows Server host run isolated virtual machines by placing a hypervisor layer between hardware and guest operating systems. Host hardware, virtual switches, storage and management remain infrastructure responsibilities; each guest still requires its own operating-system administration.
quick_check: Why is a Hyper-V host failure different from an individual guest operating-system failure?

title: Hyper-V Architecture, Hardware Requirements and Host Readiness
summary: Validate CPU virtualization, SLAT, DEP, memory and feature-specific requirements before enabling Hyper-V on Windows Server.
objective: Explain the Hyper-V host architecture and perform an evidence-based readiness review before role installation.
body_outline: Hyper-V in Windows Server is a type-1 hypervisor and is intended for enterprise virtualization workloads.
Host requirements exceed the general Windows Server minimums and include hardware-assisted virtualization, SLAT and hardware-enforced DEP; feature-specific requirements must also be checked.
Capacity planning must include CPU, memory, storage and network headroom for host operations, failover and maintenance rather than sizing only for average guest consumption.
Role installation should follow approved change control and vendor/platform support matrices.
quick_check: Why is meeting Windows Server minimum hardware specification insufficient evidence that a server is production-ready for Hyper-V?

title: Hyper-V Host, VM and Failure-Domain Architecture
summary: Model Hyper-V dependencies across host hardware, hypervisor, virtual machine configuration, guest operating system, storage and network layers.
architecture_notes: A virtualization incident should be classified by failure domain before remediation: physical host, hypervisor/host OS, VM configuration, guest OS, storage path, virtual switch or upstream network. Multiple VM failures on one host increase the probability of a shared infrastructure dependency rather than simultaneous unrelated guest faults.
enterprise_design_notes: Define host standard, firmware baseline, networking, storage, monitoring, maintenance capacity and recovery boundaries before scaling a Hyper-V estate.

title: Read-Only Hyper-V Host Readiness Evidence Pack
summary: Collect virtualization capability, Windows feature and host resource evidence before enabling or modifying Hyper-V.
objective: Produce a timestamped host-readiness pack without installing roles or changing firmware settings.
steps: Record Windows Server edition, version and build.
Run Systeminfo and capture the Hyper-V Requirements section where applicable.
Record CPU and installed memory capacity.
Inspect whether the Hyper-V role is already installed without changing feature state.
Document vendor hardware/firmware support evidence and outstanding readiness gaps.
expected_result: A read-only evidence set identifying whether host prerequisites are satisfied and what remains to be validated.

title: Hyper-V Role or VM Startup Failure: Evidence-First Decision Tree
summary: Separate hardware capability, role state, host resource and guest-specific causes before making configuration changes.
diagnostic_order: Define whether the failure affects role installation, all VMs, one VM or one guest workload.
Confirm hardware virtualization requirements and current Hyper-V role state.
Capture host memory, CPU, storage and relevant event evidence at the failure time.
Compare shared failures across VMs to identify a host, network or storage dependency.
Escalate firmware, driver or platform changes only after preserving evidence and confirming supportability.
escalation_boundary: Do not enable firmware virtualization settings, install roles, change drivers or reboot a production host without approved change and outage controls.

title: Hyper-V Virtual Switch and Network Design Foundations
summary: Design VM connectivity using virtual switches and virtual adapters while preserving host management, live-migration and workload traffic requirements.
objective: Explain virtual-switch architecture and identify network design dependencies for production Hyper-V hosts.
body_outline: Hyper-V networking connects a VM virtual network adapter to a virtual switch, which in turn connects to Ethernet-based networks.
Production design must account for management, VM workload, cluster, storage and live-migration traffic rather than treating all traffic as one undifferentiated uplink.
NIC, VLAN, QoS, redundancy and upstream-switch design should be validated end to end before host commissioning.
A connectivity incident should be traced from guest adapter to virtual switch, host uplink and upstream network instead of assuming the guest is at fault.
quick_check: Why can a healthy guest IP configuration still fail if the Hyper-V virtual-switch or upstream VLAN path is wrong?

title: Hyper-V Foundation Assessment
summary: Scenario assessment covering host readiness, failure domains and virtual-switch reasoning.

assessment_items.question: Several VMs on one host lose network connectivity simultaneously. What shared dependencies should be checked before troubleshooting each guest independently?
assessment_items.answer: The host virtual switch, physical uplinks, VLAN configuration, upstream network path and host-level health should be checked first because they are shared failure domains.

assessment_items.question: Why should Hyper-V capacity planning include maintenance and failover headroom?
assessment_items.answer: A production estate must tolerate host maintenance or failure without immediately exhausting CPU, memory, storage or network capacity on remaining hosts.

assessment_items.question: What evidence should precede Hyper-V role installation?
assessment_items.answer: Supported hardware and firmware, virtualization capability, Windows Server version/edition, host sizing, storage/network design and an approved change plan.

title: Senior Hyper-V Interview: Host Readiness and Virtual Network Architecture
summary: Senior scenarios testing virtualization failure-domain reasoning, supportability and production-change discipline.

questions.question: How would you decide whether a new physical server is ready to join a production Hyper-V estate?
answer_points: confirm CPU/memory sizing and failover headroom
confirm monitoring, backup and recovery integration
use controlled commissioning and rollback gates

questions.question: Ten VMs on one host report packet loss after a switch change. What is your troubleshooting sequence?
answer_points: avoid guest-by-guest configuration churn until shared dependencies are eliminated

questions.question: Why should host and guest operational responsibilities be separated?
answer_points: host changes can affect many workloads
guest remediation should not mask platform faults
